For nonnegative countable families, sums preserve inequalities and split over addition; for T⊆N, sum_{i in T}2^(-i-1)≤1. Consequently sum_{i in T}(rho_i+epsilon 2^(-i-1))≤sum_{i in T}rho_i+epsilon. For fixed C in [0,infinity], if 1≤C+epsilon for every real epsilon>0, then C≥1.

grounds.reason: lambda is the standard Lebesgue measure.
T⊆N, rho_i≥0, epsilon>0, and I⊆union J_i.
V,T,rho remain independent of epsilon; M005 supplies the countable union bound.

R006.justification: Countable additivity on disjoint sets yields monotonicity by splitting B as A and B\A, and yields the outer-measure union inequality by disjointification; thus a measure satisfies the structure stipulated by M005. Nonnegative series are suprema of finite partial sums, so comparison and addition follow by finite sums and cofinal finite unions. The geometric partial sums of 2^(-i-1), starting at i=0, are 1-2^(-m), with supremum 1; a subseries is no larger. If C is finite and C<1, choosing epsilon=(1-C)/2 contradicts 1≤C+epsilon; the infinite case already satisfies C≥1.

R006.fact: For fixed finite c>0 and nonnegative terms x_i,y_i, x_i≥c y_i for every i implies sum_i x_i≥c sum_i y_i, with the usual extended nonnegative interpretation. If every admissible cover cost is at least b, its infimum is at least b. If H_delta is unbounded over positive delta, sup_{delta>0}H_delta=infinity.

grounds.reason: c=delta^(s-1) is finite positive; x_i=rho_i^s, y_i=rho_i, and F003 gives sum_i y_i≥1.

R006.justification: Finite-sum comparison followed by the supremum over finite subsets proves the series inequality; multiplication by a fixed positive finite constant commutes with that supremum, including an infinite value. The infimum statement is the defining greatest-lower-bound property (also valid for an empty family); the supremum statement is its corresponding least-upper-bound property. These justify the existing cover-to-content and content-to-measure steps.

R006.fact: For d in [0,infinity], bounds d≤a for every real a>1 and d≥s for every real 0<s<1 imply d=1.

grounds.reason: N001 and the equal-interval covers give d=dimH(I)≤a for every a>1.
N001 and the divergent lower costs give d≥s for every s in (0,1).

R006.justification: The upper bounds imply d is finite, for example d≤2. If d>1, choose a=(1+d)/2, contradicting d≤a. If 0≤d<1, choose s=(1+d)/2, contradicting d≥s. Hence both d≤1 and d≥1 hold, exactly as S001 and S005 conclude.

R006.fact: For 0<s<1 and 0<x≤d with d>0, x^(s-1)≥d^(s-1), so x^s≥d^(s-1)x. For x=0 both sides of the latter inequality are zero. Also d^(s-1) is unbounded as d>0 decreases to zero.

R006.justification: Writing q=1-s>0 gives x^(s-1)=1/x^q. Positive powers are increasing, so reciprocals give the required reversed inequality. Positive-exponent powers at zero are zero. For every M>0, choosing 0<d<M^(-1/q) gives d^(s-1)>M, which justifies the later unbounded-scale conclusion without a limit exchange.

parameters.type: natural number (the nonnegative integer index of the Euclidean ambient space)

definitions.definition: For each nonnegative integer k, Eucl(k)=R^k is the space of real k-tuples, with distance (sum_{j=1}^k |x_j-y_j|^2)^(1/2) and its Borel sigma algebra. The empty tuple is the sole point of Eucl(0). Eucl(k)×R is identified with Eucl(k+1) by adjoining the last coordinate; this identification uses the Euclidean distance sqrt(||x-y||_2^2+|t-u|^2).

definitions.type: diameter function on subsets of metric or extended metric spaces
definitions.definition: diam(A)=sup{dist(x,y): x,y in A}, as an extended nonnegative number, with supremum of the empty set zero. Thus diam(empty)=0. In ordinary Euclidean spaces a nonempty set of diameter zero is a singleton. Native ediam is this extended-valued diameter. Euclidean finite diameters are identified with their nonnegative real values.

binders.type: subset of a metric or extended metric space

definitions.type: positive exponent and scale Hausdorff contents and limiting Hausdorff measure on Euclidean sets
definitions.definition:
For a Euclidean set \(A\), exponent \(s>0\), and scale \(\delta>0\), put

\[
H^s_\delta(A)=\inf\left\{\sum_i(\operatorname{diam}U_i)^s:
 A\subseteq\bigcup_iU_i,\quad\operatorname{diam}U_i\leq\delta\right\},
\qquad H^s(A)=\sup_{\delta>0}H^s_\delta(A).
\]

Covers are countable, with empty members contributing zero.

binders.type: countable family of subsets of the same Euclidean space

definitions.type: real exponent → Borel Hausdorff measure on any extended metric space
definitions.definition: muH(a) denotes the native unnormalized Borel Hausdorff measure MeasureTheory.Measure.hausdorffMeasure a. It is obtained by the metric outer-measure construction mkMetric with gauge r↦r^a on extended nonnegative diameters: at each positive scale take the maximal outer measure bounded by the gauge on all nonempty sets of at most that diameter, then take the supremum over scales and its Borel-measure realization. Values on arbitrary sets mean outer-measure values. Empty covering members cost zero and nonempty members cost diam^a with extended nonnegative-real powers; at a=0 a nonempty singleton has cost 1.

definitions.type: Hausdorff dimension of subsets of metric spaces, valued in [0,infinity]
definitions.definition: dimH(A), also written dim_H A, is the standard Hausdorff dimension: sup({a≥0 : muH(a)(A)=infinity}) in [0,infinity], where the supremum of an empty set is 0. This is the native dimH definition. The notation uses the empty-set dimension convention 0. Critical-exponent properties and agreement with the supplied positive-exponent diameter-cost measure are proof obligations, not extra assumptions.

definitions.definition: F=E×I under the Euclidean identification in D001.
D=dimH(E), initially an extended nonnegative real. Real arithmetic involving D is used only after its finiteness is proved.

definitions.type: Lebesgue measure on R and associated integral notation
definitions.definition: lambda is the standard Lebesgue measure on R with its Borel measurable structure and the normalization by interval length. For a Borel set J, |J| denotes lambda(J). The symbol 1_J denotes its indicator, equal to 1 on J and 0 elsewhere. Integrals of nonnegative functions are extended Lebesgue integrals (native lintegral). Restriction to I is lambda restricted to [0,1]. The usual interval values are lambda(I)=1 and lambda((a,b))=b-a for a<b; only these interval values are used.

argument.text: Fix k,A and a. For a>0 apply M002 with X=Eucl(k), exponent a and set A. At each finite positive scale r every admissible set has finite diameter, so its native extended diameter power is exactly the real diameter power in H; an empty member costs 0 in both conventions, and 0^a=0. Finite families may be padded by empty sets, and any countable family can be enumerated by N (with empty padding when necessary). The additional scale r=infinity in M002 cannot increase the supremum over finite positive scales: its infimum is at most the infimum at any finite scale. Thus M002 gives H^a(A)=muH(a)(A). This argument is for every a>0.

produces.statement: For every positive real v, H^v(A)=muH(v)(A).

argument.text: Under temporary premise L1: a<dimH(A), M003 gives muH(a)(A)=infinity, and F001 converts this to H^a(A)=infinity. Discharge L1, retaining that implication. Under temporary premise L2: a>dimH(A), M004 gives muH(a)(A)=0, and F001 converts this to H^a(A)=0. Discharge L2, retaining that implication. Eucl(k) has its Borel measurable structure by definition, and the arbitrary a>0 supplies the nonnegative-real source exponent in both applications. Universal introduction of a>0 yields the two clauses in F002.

produces.statement: For every v>0, v<dimH(A) implies H^v(A)=infinity, and dimH(A)<v implies H^v(A)=0.

argument.text: For a>0, if H^a(A)=0, the alternative dimH(A)>a contradicts the infinite-measure clause of F002. Thus dimH(A)≤a. If H^a(A)=infinity, the alternative dimH(A)<a contradicts the zero-measure clause, hence dimH(A)≥a. Nonnegativity follows from the [0,infinity]-valued supremum defining dimH. All these are implications with their displayed antecedents retained, not extra ambient assumptions. Since k,A and a>0 were arbitrary, universally quantify them to record F003, the full normalization and critical-exponent statements for every Euclidean set and positive exponent.

produces.statement: For every nonnegative integer k0, every Z⊆Eucl(k0) and every v>0: H^v(Z)=muH(v)(Z); v<dimH(Z) implies H^v(Z)=infinity; dimH(Z)<v implies H^v(Z)=0; H^v(Z)=0 implies dimH(Z)≤v; H^v(Z)=infinity implies dimH(Z)≥v; and dimH(Z)≥0.

argument.text: Under the temporary premise L3: A⊆B, every delta-cover of B is a delta-cover of A, whence H^v_delta(A)≤H^v_delta(B) and H^v(A)≤H^v(B), for every v>0. If dimH(A)>dimH(B), choose a positive real exponent strictly between them; this is possible also if dimH(A)=infinity, since the smaller dimension must then be finite. The critical statements just established would give infinity=H^v(A)≤H^v(B)=0, a contradiction. This proves dimension monotonicity, discharging L3 with the antecedent A⊆B retained.

Under L4: g:A→Eucl(l) preserves distances, intersect each ambient cover with A, map its members by g, and use these images to cover g(A). Conversely intersect a cover of g(A) with g(A) and take inverse images under g. Distance preservation makes g injective, and both constructions do not increase any member's diameter. Thus the two H^v_delta contents, and then the two H^v measures, are equal for every v>0 and delta>0. The same between-exponents contradiction as in S004 shows dimH(g(A))=dimH(A). This also treats empty A, whose contents vanish and dimension is 0. Discharge L4 and quantify k,A,l,g and retain each stated conditional premise to obtain every clause of the exported claim.

For the grid construction fix 0<h≤1.

argument.text: H003 says E is compact. Compact subsets of Euclidean space are bounded: the open balls centered at the origin with positive integer radii cover the space, so a finite subcover of E puts it inside one such ball. Hence there exists a real L>0 with E⊆[-L,L]^n. Record this existence before choosing L.

produces.statement: There exists L0>0 such that E⊆[-L0,L0]^n.

argument.text: Choose L as in F001 and set C=(2L+2)^n. By H001, n≥0; first take the branch L1: n≥1. For 0<h≤1, divide each coordinate interval [-L,L] into at most ceil(2L/h) closed intervals of length at most h. The resulting grid contains at most (2L/h+1)^n≤C h^(-n) cubes, each of diameter at most sqrt(n) h, and covers E. For any s>n the total s-cost is at most C n^(s/2) h^(s-n), which tends to zero as h decreases to zero. At each fixed target scale take h≤delta/sqrt(n) and then h arbitrarily small; H^s_delta(E)=0 at every scale, hence H^s(E)=0. N001 yields D≤s for every s>n, so D≤n. N001 also gives 0≤D. This proves the branch L1 implication; discharge L1.

produces.statement: If n≥1, then 0≤D≤n.

argument.text: For the other branch L2: n=0, H002 and the single empty tuple give E=Eucl(0), a singleton. A singleton cover has diameter 0 and zero s-cost for every s>0, so H^s(E)=0 for all s>0. N001 gives D≤s for every s>0, and D≥0, hence D=0. Discharge L2. Since the nonnegative integer n is either zero or at least one, the two branches and F002 give 0≤D≤n, in particular finite D.

produces.statement: 0≤D≤n and D is finite.

argument.text: Finally let s>0 and delta>0. The family of open balls centered at points of E with radius delta/4 covers E. By H003 it has a finite subcover. Each such ball has diameter at most delta/2≤delta, and its s-cost is finite; for n=0 its diameter is 0. Thus this finite admissible cover has finite total cost, so H^s_delta(E)<infinity. Together with F003 this is the exported claim.

argument.text: First consider L1: n=0. N002 gives D=0. H002 and the fact that Eucl(0) has one point imply E=Eucl(0), so F is isometric to I. For any a>1, divide I into N equal closed intervals, where N ranges through the positive integers. Their corresponding copies in F have diameter 1/N, total a-cost N(1/N)^a=N^(1-a) tending to zero, and mesh tending to zero. Thus H^a(F)=0: at each fixed delta, sufficiently large N are admissible and their costs tend to zero. N001 gives dimH(F)≤a for every a>1, hence dimH(F)≤1=D+1. Discharge L1.

argument.text: For the remaining branch introduce L2: n≥1, and fix q with temporary premise L3: q>D. N002 gives D≥0, so q>0. N001 gives H^q(E)=0 and therefore H^q_r(E)=0 at any r>0. For arbitrary r in (0,1] and epsilon>0, the infimum defining H^q_r supplies a countable r-cover of cost <epsilon/2. Discard empty members. Each nonempty member of diameter zero is a singleton. Replace its i-th occurrence by a Euclidean ball centered at that singleton, of positive diameter ≤r and q-cost <epsilon 2^(-i-2). Such a ball exists since n≥1, and arbitrarily small positive radii have positive diameter and q-cost tending to zero. Keep the other members. Their total cost is <epsilon/2+epsilon sum_{i≥0}2^(-i-2)=epsilon. This proves existence of a countable cover of E by nonempty members with positive diameters ≤r and total q-cost <epsilon.

produces.statement: q>0, and there exists a countable cover U0 of E by nonempty subsets of Eucl(n) such that 0<diam(U0_i)≤r for every member and sum_i diam(U0_i)^q<epsilon.

argument.text: Choose U from F002; set r_i=diam(U_i) and N_i=ceil(1/r_i). Partition I into N_i equal closed intervals of length 1/N_i≤r_i. Since 0<r_i≤r≤1, N_i≤1/r_i+1≤2/r_i. Let W be the family of products of U_i with these intervals. It is countable, being a countable union of finite families, and covers F. For any two points in a member of W, the squared Euclidean distance is at most r_i^2+r_i^2. Thus each member has diameter ≤sqrt(2) r_i≤sqrt(2) r.

produces.statement: W is a countable cover of F, its members over U_i have diameter at most sqrt(2) r_i, and N_i≤2/r_i.

argument.text: Using F003 and q>0, the total (q+1)-cost of W is at most sum_i N_i(sqrt(2) r_i)^(q+1) ≤ 2(sqrt(2))^(q+1) sum_i r_i^q < 2(sqrt(2))^(q+1) epsilon. All terms are nonnegative, so termwise inequalities and the countable grouping are valid even before finiteness is known; the last strict inequality supplies finiteness. Since r and epsilon were arbitrary and the private U does not occur in the assertion, this proves: for every r0 in (0,1] and every e0>0, F has a countable cover of mesh ≤sqrt(2) r0 and (q+1)-cost <2(sqrt(2))^(q+1)e0.

produces.statement: For every r0 in (0,1] and every e0>0 there exists a countable cover of F with member diameters ≤sqrt(2)r0 and (q+1)-cost <2(sqrt(2))^(q+1)e0.

argument.text: For an arbitrary delta>0 set r_star=min(1,delta/sqrt(2))>0. Apply F004 with r0=r_star and arbitrary e0>0. The resulting covers are delta-admissible and their (q+1)-cost is less than 2(sqrt(2))^(q+1)e0. Let e0 decrease to zero, keeping q and delta fixed; hence H^{q+1}_delta(F)=0. Since delta was arbitrary, H^{q+1}(F)=0. N001 gives dimH(F)≤q+1.

argument.text: Discharge L3 and universally quantify q: for every q>D, dimH(F)≤q+1. Discharge L2, proving the n≥1 branch. Together with F001 and the exhaustive alternatives n=0 or n≥1, this proves the exported claim.

Thus A_i and B_i are nonempty and have diameter ≤rho_i≤delta. In particular B_i is bounded, with finite infimum and supremum and sup B_i-inf B_i≤rho_i. Put c=H^s_delta(E). By N002, c is finite.

argument.text: For arbitrary epsilon>0 set eta_i=epsilon 2^(-i-1)/(1+rho_i^s)>0. By F001 define the bounded open interval J_i=(inf B_i-eta_i/2,sup B_i+eta_i/2). It contains B_i and its length is sup B_i-inf B_i+eta_i≤rho_i+eta_i. This construction also works when rho_i=0. No measurability of V_i, A_i or B_i is asserted or required. argument.text: For each t∈I, the A_i with t∈J_i cover E. Indeed, for each x∈E, the point (x,t)∈F lies in some V_i, so x∈A_i and t∈B_i⊆J_i. Their diameters are ≤rho_i≤delta by F001. Each f_i is a nonnegative Borel measurable function: J_i is open and the coefficient rho_i^s is finite. Thus it is almost-everywhere measurable for lambda restricted to I.

argument.text: Integrate F003 over I, whose Lebesgue measure is one. Monotonicity of the nonnegative integral gives c≤integral_I sum_i f_i. argument.text: For any a>1, the N equal closed subintervals of I, with N a positive integer, have diameter 1/N and total a-cost N^(1-a) tending to zero, while their mesh tends to zero. At each fixed scale they are eventually admissible with arbitrarily small cost, so H^a(I)=0. By N001, dimH(I)≤a for every a>1 and hence dimH(I)≤1.

argument.text: For the lower estimate fix 0<s<1 and delta>0. Let V be any countable family and introduce L1: it is a delta-cover of I. Enumerate with empty padding and let T⊆N index the nonempty members. Put rho_i=diam(V_i)≤delta. Each V_i is a bounded nonempty subset of R, so sup V_i-inf V_i=rho_i. For any epsilon>0 define J_i=(inf V_i-epsilon 2^(-i-2),sup V_i+epsilon 2^(-i-2)). These open intervals contain V_i and have length rho_i+epsilon 2^(-i-1). Thus they cover I and are Borel measurable.

produces.statement: I⊆union_{i in T}J_i, and each J_i is an open bounded interval of length rho_i+epsilon 2^(-i-1).

argument.text: Apply M005 to Lebesgue measure lambda, the countable index type T, and the intervals J_i. Measure monotonicity and F002 yield 1=lambda(I)≤lambda(union_i J_i)≤sum_i lambda(J_i)=sum_i(rho_i+epsilon 2^(-i-1))≤sum_i rho_i+epsilon. If sum_i rho_i is infinite then sum_i rho_i≥1 already; otherwise let epsilon decrease to zero. The V,rho and T do not depend on epsilon, so sum_i rho_i≥1 in all cases.

argument.text: Because 0<s<1 and 0≤rho_i≤delta, rho_i^s≥delta^(s-1)rho_i: for rho_i>0 divide by rho_i and use the decreasing power with negative exponent s-1; for rho_i=0 both sides are zero. Hence sum_i rho_i^s≥delta^(s-1)sum_i rho_i≥delta^(s-1) by F003. Discharge L1 and take the infimum over all delta-covers V. This proves H^s_delta(I)≥delta^(s-1) for every delta>0.

argument.text: Since s-1<0, delta^(s-1) tends to infinity as delta decreases to zero, and F004 implies H^s(I)=infinity. By N001, dimH(I)≥s for every s∈(0,1). Letting s increase to 1 gives dimH(I)≥1. Combining with F001 proves dimH(I)=1, with no missing zero-dimensional ambient case.

argument.text: H002 supplies a point x0∈E. Define g:I→Eucl(n+1) by g(t)=(x0,t). The Euclidean distance between g(t) and g(u) is sqrt(0+|t-u|^2)=|t-u|, so g preserves distances. Its image is contained in F by x0∈E and the definition F=E×I. N001 gives dimH(g(I))=dimH(I) and dimH(F)≥dimH(g(I)). N006 gives dimH(I)=1, hence dimH(F)≥1. Under the temporary premise L1: D=0, this reads dimH(F)≥1=D+1. Discharge L1; x0 is absent from the output. This proves the exported claim for all n, including n=0.

N002 gives the finite real value D≥0, so either D>0 or D=0. N005 gives dimH(F)≥D+1 in the first case, and N007 gives the same bound in the second. Case elimination therefore gives dimH(F)≥D+1 unconditionally. N003 gives the reverse bound, so dimH(F)=D+1. Substituting F=E×I, I=[0,1] and D=dimH(E), with the Euclidean product identification of D001, yields dim_H(E×[0,1])=dim_H E+1. These bounds apply for every original nonempty compact E⊆R^n and every n≥0, as required.

full_target:
Here dimension means **Hausdorff dimension**. As approved by the user on
2026-10-23, assume explicitly that \(E\) is nonempty. With the convention
\(\dim_H\varnothing=0\), the printed equality would otherwise fail for
the empty set. This is a disclosed addition to the printed exercise.

Let \(n\geq0\) be an integer, let \(E\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty
compact set, and put \(I=[0,1]\). Identify \(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\)
with \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) and use its Euclidean metric. Prove

\[
\dim_H(E\times[0,1])=\dim_H E+1.
\]

The zero-dimensional ambient space \(\mathbb R^0\) is included. A later
formalization using a different product norm must justify the metric change.
